chunks.section: Optimizer Geometry Sets the Pace: Spectral Learning Dynamics in Matrix Factorization
chunks.text: Mahalakshmi Sabanayagam Simon Lucey Affiliation: Australian Institute for Machine Learning, Adelaide University Affiliation: {mahalakshmi.sabanayagam, simon.lucey}@adelaide.edu.au

Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

For much of modern deep learning, large scale optimization was dominated by SGD and Adam-like coordinate-wise methods, while matrix preconditioning and approximate curvature methods remained comparatively limited in practice. Their additional memory, numerical, and systems requirements made their advantages difficult to realize at scale ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ; Gupta et al., 2018 ) . This landscape is beginning to change. Recent foundation models with multi-billion and trillion parameters ( Team et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Khona et al., 2026 ; Ji et al., 2026 ) are effectively trained with spectral optimizers such as Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) and SOAP ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) at substantially large model, data, and batch scales. This empirical shift raises a theoretical question. The implicit bias analysis of gradient descent (GD) shows that Euclidean geometry slows the progress of weak singular modes and thereby promotes low-rank solutions in deep matrix factorization ( Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ) . Whereas spectral normalization and curvature correction are designed to reduce precisely this kind of anisotropy, in idealized limits they can weaken or even cancel the singular value dependent slowdown. Their recent success therefore raises the question of whether GD’s spectral bias induced by depth is lost, preserved in a weaker form, or replaced by a qualitatively different mechanism of mode selection. More broadly, we ask: When do modern optimizers merely accelerate a common learning trajectory, and when do they change which spectral components emerge, persist, or disappear?

We investigate these questions in deep linear networks, where depth changes the parameterization and optimization dynamics without changing the end-to-end linear functions. This makes it a particularly clean setting for separating optimizer-induced dynamics from parameterization-induced bias. Our theoretical analysis focuses on deep matrix factorization, a canonical special case in which the evolution of singular modes can be characterized explicitly. Specifically, in full observation regression, it exposes transient singular mode learning ( Saxe et al., 2013 ; Soudry et al., 2018 ) , while in underdetermined matrix sensing and completion, it permits direct study of which interpolating matrix is selected ( Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Rhee et al., 2026 ; Parviz et al., 2026 ) .

In contrast to the Euclidean geometry of GD, non-Euclidean optimizers transform the factorization-induced geometry in qualitatively different ways. SignGD and Adam apply coordinate-wise adaptive scaling ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ; Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) ; Muon acts directly on the spectrum of matrix updates ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) while Shampoo introduces history-dependent matrix preconditioning ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) ; and K-FAC attempts to compensate for the parameterization through curvature using approximate natural gradients ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ) . In our study, we categorize these geometries based on their updates into Euclidean (GD), coordinate-wise (SignGD and Adam), spectral (Muon and Shampoo) and curvature based (K-FAC). These methods can reach nearly identical training losses while producing weights with different spectra, representations, and performance. Recent studies have begun to identify optimizer-dependent feature and simplicity biases, including differences between Adam and GD in nonlinear models ( Cattaneo et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Xie and Li, 2024 ) and between spectral and Euclidean updates in deep linear networks ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) . These findings further motivate the central question we posed, and answering this requires distinguishing how quickly modes emerge from how they settle or disappear, since an optimizer can affect these phases differently. (a) GD (b) Muon (c) GD vs Muon: Birth and decay

Figure 1: Optimizer geometry sets the pace of spectral learning. In balanced aligned deep matrix factorization, GD and Muon produce distinct spectral learning trajectories (experimental details in App. F ). (a) Under GD, larger target modes are learned earlier, while smaller modes remain suppressed for longer. (b) Under Muon, factor amplitudes grow at a common speed, allowing smaller targets to reach full recovery earlier. (c) From the same initial amplitude 0.01 0.01 , Muon accelerates the growth of a positive target mode (red) and, importantly, removes the zero target mode in finite time (blue). GD instead exhibits delayed growth and slow decay. Thus, faster emergence of weak modes does not imply weaker removal of unsupported modes. Optimizer geometry determines which spectral components emerge, persist, and disappear. Other optimizers are discussed in later sections.

Our approach separates the geometry induced by the factorization from the update rule and state maintained by the optimizer. The product dynamics first express how each layer updates combine into the dynamics of the effective matrix. Under explicit balance, target alignment, and state compatibility assumptions, this description reduces to a common equation for each singular mode. The factorization determines how factor dynamics changes the mode amplitude, while the optimizer determines the update through its normalization, accumulated statistics, and damping. This gives a controlled setting in which these mechanisms can be compared without attributing differences to changing singular directions. Our analysis separates three aspects of spectral learning that are often conflated: the birth of initially small nonzero modes to reach a prescribed amplitude, saturation near their targets, and decay of unsupported modes whose target is zero. These phases need not respond to an optimizer in the same way. A method can permit rapid emergence while retaining a slow decay tail, and accumulated gradient history can change the rate at which an already learned component settles. Consequently, the emergence of small modes alone does not describe the spectral bias of an entire trajectory as studied in prior works. Our results make these distinctions explicit as shown in Fig. 1 . Moreover, it also brings out how optimizer state parameters, including adaptive stabilization and curvature damping, interpolate between distinct rank selection regimes, and verifies that these differences persist in underdetermined matrix factorization and regression. We express effective matrix dynamics through the layer updates and derive an exact mode reduction under explicit balance and alignment assumptions. The reduction separates the contribution of the factorization from the optimizer update states.

( 𝟐 ) \mathbf{(2)} Phase laws revealing how optimizer settings shape the bias of depth. We derive birth, saturation, and decay laws that distinguish normalization, accumulated history, and damping. GD and SignGD dynamics establish contrasting reference behaviors. Instantaneous Adam identifies how a positive stabilizer restores slow dynamics at small gradient magnitudes. Ideal Muon accelerates both emergence and removal of modes in finite time. For cumulative Shampoo, an exact accumulator identity quantifies the transition from initialization dominated to history dominated dynamics. For the specified K-FAC block model, an exact birth time decomposition separates an undamped contribution from a damping-weighted GD contribution. Together, these results identify when optimizer geometry preserves, modifies, or cancels the suppression of small modes induced by depth. ( 𝟑 ) \mathbf{(3)} Numerical validation of phase laws and regime transitions. Controlled experiments in deep matrix factorization and regression verify the derived phase laws. These experiments demonstrate that settings commonly associated with numerical stability can change relative spectral progress, determining which components emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Optimization geometry influences which solution is selected among those that fit the training data ( Wilson et al., 2017 ; Gunasekar et al., 2018 ) . For Adam, implicit bias analyses establish margin characterizations in separable classification under specified optimizer and learning rate assumptions ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Gronich and Vardi, 2026 ) . Natural gradient provides another illustration of the role of geometry: under suitable rank conditions, its effective matrix dynamics can eliminate the dependence on depth that arises under Euclidean gradient flow ( Kerekes et al., 2021 ; Bernacchia et al., 2018 ) . These results motivate examining both the symmetries respected by an optimizer and the trajectory it induces. Our framework complements this perspective by expressing changes in unobserved matrix directions through accumulated optimizer induced motion, while using mode dynamics to isolate the effects of different optimizers.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

chunks.section: 4 A Common Framework for Optimizer Geometry
chunks.text: We develop a common framework to compare how optimizer geometry controls the emergence, growth, and decay of singular modes. To derive explicit phase laws, we adopt the training dynamics analysis that connects low rank learning to the evolution of the effective matrix spectrum and consider a balanced, aligned setting in which singular directions remain fixed ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ) . This construction follows the exact mode analysis of deep linear networks ( Saxe et al., 2013 ) and isolates the effects of different optimizer geometries. We consider full observation with ℒ ( W ) = 1 2 ∥ W L ⋯ W 1 − M ∥ F 2 \mathcal{L}(W)=\frac{1}{2}\|W_{L}\cdots W_{1}-M\|_{F}^{2} , and the gradient G = W − M . G=W-M. chunks.section: Verification of the phase laws in Theorem 2 .
chunks.text: Fig. 2 compares quantities measured from the trajectories with the theoretical predictions. For birth, GD retains exponent p p , ideal Muon follows q q , instantaneous Adam interpolates between the Euclidean and normalized regimes, cumulative Shampoo moves from p p toward its history-adapted exponent p − 1 p-1 , and undamped K-FAC removes the singular-magnitude dependence with α b = 0 \alpha_{\mathrm{b}}=0 . The decay curves distinguish finite extinction under ideal Muon, exponential decay under undamped K-FAC, and the polynomial tails of GD and cumulative Shampoo. The saturation experiment further reveals optimizer-dependent mode ordering: GD and Adam converge faster for larger targets; undamped K-FAC is approximately target independent while Muon shows dependence; history-dominated Shampoo reverses the GD ordering. Thus the optimizers change relative spectral progress rather than merely rescaling a common trajectory. Figure 2: Verification of the phase laws in Theorem 2 at depth L = 4 L=4 . (a) The birth exponent α b \alpha_{\mathrm{b}} separates Euclidean, normalized, history adapted, and curvature corrected dynamics. (b) The decay exponent α d \alpha_{\mathrm{d}} distinguishes finite extinction of Muon ( α d = q < 1 \alpha_{\mathrm{d}}\!=\!q\!<\!1 ) from the other optimizers. (c) The saturation coefficient β \beta reveals target dependent mode ordering. (a) Adam ϵ \epsilon controls the regime (b) Two phases of Shampoo (c) K-FAC λ KF > 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}\!>\!0 restores barrier Figure 3: Optimizer state parameters control the local birth regime. Adam’s stability parameter ϵ \epsilon shifts the GD-to-SignGD crossover; Shampoo damping delays the transition from p p to p − 1 p-1 ; and K-FAC damping restores the GD exponent below its curvature threshold.

Fig. 3 varies the state parameters determined in Theorem 2 that separate the local regimes. For instantaneous Adam, decreasing ϵ \epsilon moves the transition from the GD exponent p p to the SignGD exponent q q toward smaller modes. Large ϵ \epsilon retains the Euclidean exponent over a wider range of mode amplitudes, whereas small ϵ \epsilon yields the normalized exponent q q almost immediately. For cumulative Shampoo, decreasing λ Sh \lambda_{\mathrm{Sh}} causes accumulated history to dominate earlier, advancing the transition from p p to p − 1 p-1 . For K-FAC, positive damping restores the GD exponent when σ p ≪ λ KF , \sigma^{p}\ll\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}, whereas curvature correction removes the barrier when σ p ≫ λ KF . \sigma^{p}\gg\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}. As λ KF → 0 \lambda_{\rm KF}\rightarrow 0 , this transition moves toward smaller amplitudes, recovering the undamped K-FAC regime. These experiments confirm that stabilization, accumulated state, and damping determine which phase law governs a mode at a given spectral scale.

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

Generative AI tools were used to assist with language polishing, related work discovery, and selected coding and debugging tasks. They were not used to draft complete sections or to generate mathematical proofs. All proofs were developed by the authors, although AI tools were occasionally used to check arguments and suggest clearer formulations. Example use cases include code for plotting, logging, and refactoring the functions which were all verified to do what was intended. All references, code, and final text were independently verified and thoroughly reviewed by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content.

This work is theoretical and empirical research on optimization dynamics in deep matrix factorization. It does not involve human participants, personal or sensitive data, or deployment in high-stakes decision-making settings. The experiments primarily use controlled synthetic matrix factorization and regression problems designed to derive deeper insights about the optimizer behavior. Thus, we believe the potential benefits of this research outweigh its risks. Additionally, we do not see any immediate risk stemming from our work.

We state all assumptions, optimizer conventions, continuous-time update rules, and initialization conditions used in the theoretical analysis. Complete derivations and proofs are provided in the appendix, including the effective-matrix dynamics, aligned-mode reduction, and birth, decay, and saturation laws. For the experiments, we specify the data, depth, balanced initialization, optimizer hyperparameters, damping and stabilization parameters, stopping criteria, and procedures used to estimate the local phase exponents in App. F and G . We provide the source code and experiment configurations needed to reproduce the reported figures and tables in the supplementary material as a zip file.

Saxe et al. (2013) derive exact learning dynamics for deep linear networks under structured initial conditions, including a decoupled mode representation and equal strengths across layers. Their analysis supplies the direct precedent for our aligned phase model. Arora et al. (2018) show that linear overparameterization changes the effective optimization geometry and can act as a preconditioner. Du et al. (2018) study balancing properties of gradient flow in homogeneous models, while Arora et al. (2019) use balanced initialization to derive effective matrix and singular value dynamics for deep matrix factorization. These GD results motivate our setup, but conservation of the GD balance invariant generally does not hold for other optimizers.

chunks.section: Low-rank bias and the limits of norm descriptions.
chunks.text: Gunasekar et al. (2017) investigate implicit regularization in two-layer matrix factorization and conjecture a nuclear-norm characterization in a restricted commuting setting. Arora et al. (2019) extend the analysis to depth and derive singular-value-dependent mobility under balanced gradient flow, showing that depth strengthens the tendency toward low-rank solutions. Razin and Cohen (2020) construct matrix-completion problems in which norms diverge as the loss vanishes, demonstrating the limits of a universal norm-minimization account. Li et al. (2021) instead develop a greedy low-rank learning interpretation under explicit assumptions. A complementary trajectory perspective is provided by Neural Tangent Kernel and lazy-training analyses, which characterize sufficiently wide networks through a linearization around initialization and an approximately fixed kernel governing function-space evolution ( Jacot et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2019 ; Sabanayagam et al., 2022 ) . In contrast, our analysis retains the nonlinear multiplicative parameterization and its evolving, optimizer-dependent spectral mobility, allowing us to compare the birth, saturation, and decay of singular modes before convergence.

Wilson et al. (2017) demonstrate that adaptive optimization can select solutions with substantially different generalization from GD even when training fit is good. Gunasekar et al. (2018) characterize implicit bias for several optimization geometries in underdetermined linear regression and separable classification. These results establish the broader principle that optimization geometry affects solution selection. Deep factorization adds a parameter dependent product differential, so the geometry acting on the effective matrix changes with both the factors and optimizer state captured by our general trajectory identity in Proposition 1 .

chunks.section: Implicit bias of Adam and related adaptive methods.
chunks.text: Cattaneo et al. (2023) use backward error analysis to characterize corrections to Adam and RMSProp dynamics, relating implicit regularization to hyperparameters and training stage. The classification literature builds on the maximum margin characterization of GD for separable data ( Soudry et al., 2018 ) . Wang et al. (2021) study limiting parameter directions in homogeneous classification under their adaptive flow assumptions. Zhang et al. (2024) establish a maximum ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} margin result for full batch Adam in separable linear classification. Xie and Li (2024) connect AdamW, which includes decoupled weight decay, to ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} -norm constrained optimization under full-batch assumptions. Vasudeva et al. (2026) analyze a difference in feature learning between Adam and GD in a Gaussian classification model with two layer ReLU networks. These results concern distinct losses, optimizer conventions, or notions of bias. Our squared loss analysis studies finite singular amplitudes and phase times without weight decay, so classification margin results do not directly determine its birth or saturation laws.

chunks.section: Analysis of spectral descent, Shampoo, Muon and K-FAC.
chunks.text: Fan et al. (2026) characterize spectral descent and Muon through margin maximization in multiclass linear classification. Chen et al. (2025) connect Muon with decoupled weight decay to spectral-norm-constrained optimization. Eschenhagen et al. (2026) interpret Shampoo as spectral descent adapted to stochasticity and the parameter trajectory. History dependence is therefore an established feature of this geometry. Our contribution is the exact first integral of the specified cumulative accumulator in the aligned factorization model and its consequences for phase times. That identity does not extend unchanged to exponential averages or different inverse powers. Kerekes et al. (2021) explicitly study natural gradient implicit bias in deep linear classification and matrix factorization. Under their Gaussian model and Jacobian rank condition, natural gradient flow for matrix completion matches direct optimization of the effective matrix, leaving unobserved entries unchanged. This is a direct precedent for connecting geometry to motion outside the observed coordinates. Our block curvature analysis quantifies the effect of additive damping on mode birth and decay, and distinguishes it from both full curvature and factored damping. These works provide important geometry and momentum precedents, while our phase laws concern squared loss, explicit stabilization or damping factors, and finite targets in factorized models.

chunks.section: Analysis of Muon in matrix factorization.
chunks.text: Kang et al. (2026) analyze spectral gradient flow in a simplified LoRA factorization setting, proving approximately equal spectral growth rates and convergence results under stated conditions. Dragutinović and Ranganath (2026) derive dynamics for simplified Muon in deep linear networks and linear attention and investigate how avoiding slow sequential learning changes simplicity bias. Rhee et al. (2026) analyze bilinear factorization with full observation, including uniform factor growth after alignment, a conserved quantity distinct from GD’s, and finite step oscillations near solutions. They also study alignment in simplified settings. These results already establish much of the ideal polar growth baseline. Our treatment places it alongside memory dependent adaptive flows and damped curvature flows, with separate statements for birth, saturation, and zero target decay. Parviz et al. (2026) report controlled optimizer comparisons showing that Muon’s relative performance in factorization depends on the problem and hyperparameter tuning. This motivates separating exact polar flow predictions from practical implementation effects and comparing recovery at a common training fit.

chunks.section: Appendix D Aligned Singular Mode Dynamics
chunks.text: In this section, we prove Theorem 1 by restricting these dynamics to the balanced and aligned mode manifold introduced in the main text. We first explain when balance is preserved, then show how balance and alignment produce a common layer amplitude, and finally derive the effective singular-mode dynamics. Throughout this section, let d ≤ min ℓ = 0 , … , L ⁡ d ℓ d\leq\min_{\ell=0,\ldots,L}d_{\ell} denote the active mode dimension. For each layer, let there be an orthogonal matrix Q ℓ ∈ ℝ d ℓ × d , Q ℓ ⊤ ​ Q ℓ = I d . Q_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell}\times d},\,Q_{\ell}^{\top}Q_{\ell}=I_{d}. All matrix identities below are understood on these active subspaces. Components in the orthogonal complements are initialized at zero and remain absent under the compatible aligned updates considered here.

chunks.section: D.5 Why the Alignment Assumption is Appropriate
chunks.text: Assumption 2 does not claim that arbitrary training trajectories become aligned with the target. It restricts the analysis to a canonical invariant subspace in which exact mode dynamics can be derived. This restriction is standard in analyses of deep linear networks and deep matrix factorization ( Saxe et al., 2013 ; Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ) . It has three useful properties. First, full-observation regression fixes a target basis through the singular directions of M M . If the factors and optimizer states are initialized in compatible chain bases, the layer gradients remain in those bases. Second, fixing the same initial spectral configuration for every optimizer ensures that differences in mode evolution arise from the optimizer update and its state, rather than from different initial singular directions. Third, the aligned model retains the nonlinear multiplicative dependence of the effective modes on the factors. It therefore preserves the depth-dependent mobility responsible for the phase laws while removing singular-vector rotation from the comparison. For spectral and curvature-based optimizers, the aligned subspace is preserved by their matrix-equivariant updates. For coordinatewise methods, the same construction is exact when the aligned basis is the parameter coordinate basis. The general matrix dynamics outside this invariant subspace are given in the previous appendix section. If the target contains repeated singular values, the singular basis is not unique within the corresponding degenerate subspace. Any fixed orthonormal basis in that subspace may be chosen as the reference basis. The theorem tracks modes in these fixed reference bases and does not require their amplitudes to remain sorted by magnitude.

chunks.section: Appendix E Optimizer Specific Phase Laws
chunks.text: In this section, we prove the phase laws for all the optimizers discussed in Sec. 5 . Theorem 1 reduces every compatible optimizer to a scalar evolution for each aligned mode. Suppressing the mode index, the effective singular amplitude satisfies σ ˙ = − L ​ σ q ​ z ​ ( σ , S ⁡ ( σ ) ) , q = 1 − 1 L , \dot{\sigma}=-L\sigma^{q}z(\sigma,S(\sigma)),\qquad q=1-\frac{1}{L}, where z z is the optimizer update coefficient and S S denotes any associated optimizer state. The state S ⁡ ( σ ) S(\sigma) may include momentum, adaptive moments, accumulated gradient covariances, or curvature estimates. Before deriving the individual optimizer results, we establish a common passage time calculus for birth, decay, and saturation. Each optimizer specific phase law then follows by identifying the local form of z z , or equivalently the local power law of σ ˙ \dot{\sigma} . This separates the universal passage time argument from the optimizer specific evolution of its internal state. We use asymptotic notations o ( . ) o(.) and O ( . ) O(.) when taking limits in the asymptotic analysis.

chunks.section: E.1 Birth, Decay, and Saturation times
chunks.text: As discussed in Sec. 5 , for a positive target μ > 0 \mu>0 , let a mode begin at σ ⁡ ( 0 ) = s > 0 . \sigma(0)=s>0. For a fixed threshold s < b < μ , s<b<\mu, the birth time is the first passage time T opt birth ​ ( s , b ) = inf { t ≥ 0 : σ ⁡ ( t ) = b } . T_{\mathrm{opt}}^{\mathrm{birth}}(s,b)=\inf\left\{t\geq 0:\sigma(t)=b\right\}. Birth always refers to escape from a positive seed s → 0 + s\to 0^{+} . It does not refer to spontaneous activation of an exactly zero factor mode. For an unsupported mode with μ = 0 , \mu=0, and a tolerance 0 < δ < s , 0<\delta<s, the decay time is T opt decay ​ ( s , δ ) = inf { t ≥ 0 : σ ⁡ ( t ) = δ } . T_{\mathrm{opt}}^{\mathrm{decay}}(s,\delta)=\inf\left\{t\geq 0:\sigma(t)=\delta\right\}. For a nonzero target, define the residual r ⁡ ( t ) = | σ ⁡ ( t ) − μ | . r(t)=|\sigma(t)-\mu|. Given a tolerance τ > 0 \tau>0 and r ⁡ ( t 0 ) = r 0 r(t_{0})=r_{0} , the saturation time is T opt sat ​ ( r 0 , τ ) = inf { u ≥ 0 : r ⁡ ( t 0 + v ) ≤ τ ​ for every ​ v ≥ u } . A closed phase law requires either solving the coupled state equations or eliminating the state through an invariant. Cumulative Shampoo admits such an elimination through its accumulator identity. The time required to reduce the residual from r 0 r_{0} to τ ∈ ( 0 , r 0 ) \tau\in(0,r_{0}) is T sat ​ ( r 0 , τ ) = { 1 β ​ log ⁡ r 0 τ , γ = 1 , r 0 1 − γ − τ 1 − γ β ⁡ ( 1 − γ ) , γ ≠ 1 . T^{\mathrm{sat}}(r_{0},\tau)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{\beta}\log\dfrac{r_{0}}{\tau},&\gamma=1,\\[8.53581pt] \dfrac{r_{0}^{1-\gamma}-\tau^{1-\gamma}}{\beta(1-\gamma)},&\gamma\neq 1.\end{cases} If γ < 1 \gamma<1 , the target is reached in finite time. If γ = 0 \gamma=0 , the residual decreases linearly: r ⁡ ( t ) = ( r 0 − β ​ t ) + , r(t)=\left(r_{0}-\beta t\right)_{+}, and β \beta is the constant residual speed. If γ = 1 \gamma=1 , the residual decreases exponentially: r ⁡ ( t ) = r 0 ​ e − β ​ t , r(t)=r_{0}e^{-\beta t}, and β \beta is the exponential saturation rate. If γ > 1 \gamma>1 , the residual has an algebraic tail: r ( t ) ∼ ( β ( γ − 1 ) t ) − 1 / ( γ − 1 ) . r(t)\sim\left(\beta(\gamma-1)t\right)^{-1/(\gamma-1)}.

T^{\mathrm{sat}}(r_{0},\tau)=\frac{1}{\beta}\int_{\tau}^{r_{0}}r^{-\gamma}\,dr. Evaluating the integral gives the passage time formula. Solving the same separated equation for r ⁡ ( t ) r(t) yields the stated trajectory laws. ∎ For γ = 0 \gamma=0 , the coefficient β \beta is a speed rather than an exponential rate. For γ = 1 \gamma=1 , it is the usual local exponential rate. For general γ \gamma , we refer to β \beta as the saturation coefficient. The scalar saturation exponent is most useful for monotone first order flows. If the optimizer state introduces overshoot or oscillation, the residual may not satisfy a closed first order equation. In that case, saturation must be analyzed through the full state dynamics, and the enter and remain definition distinguishes true saturation from a temporary crossing of the tolerance band. The optimizer specific proofs that follow therefore have two steps. First, we derive or eliminate the relevant optimizer state to identify z z along the phase. Second, we apply Propositions 3 and 4 to obtain the corresponding birth, decay, and saturation times.

Depth strongly suppresses the birth of new modes, strengthening the initialization barrier. For L > 2 L>2 , the divergence of birth time is polynomial. Thus an infinitesimally initialized singular mode takes polynomially longer to become macroscopically active. This is the primary mechanism behind sequential low-rank learning. Depth does not rapidly eliminate existing modes. Decay time diverges for all depth. Indeed: L = 1 L=1 gives an exponential tail; L > 1 L>1 gives the slower polynomial tail. Thus Euclidean GD does not produce exact finite-time rank reduction. Its low-rank bias comes mainly from preventing weak modes from being born, rather than from rapidly pruning modes that are already active.

chunks.section: Depth and the order of limits.
chunks.text: The two exponents q q and p p play different roles. The exponent q q controls the SignGD-like motion in the factor-amplitude coordinate and the locations of the crossover scales. The exponent p p controls the ϵ \epsilon -dominated birth barrier, the final decay tail, and the local exponential saturation rate. For fixed ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , increasing depth changes the birth asymptotics from logarithmic at L = 2 L=2 to polynomial at L > 2 L>2 , with exponent p − 1 = L − 2 L . p-1=\frac{L-2}{L}. The unsupported-mode decay tail has exponent p = 2 − 2 L , p=2-\frac{2}{L}, which also increases with depth. Thus deeper factorizations make the extreme small-gradient regimes increasingly resistant both to the emergence of infinitesimal positive modes and to the complete removal of already active modes. For L ≥ 2 L\geq 2 , the limits ϵ → 0 \epsilon\to 0 and s → 0 s\to 0 do not commute. For every fixed s > 0 s>0 , lim ϵ → 0 T IAdam birth ​ ( s , b ) = T SignGD birth ​ ( s , b ) . \lim_{\epsilon\to 0}T_{\mathrm{IAdam}}^{\mathrm{birth}}(s,b)=T_{\mathrm{SignGD}}^{\mathrm{birth}}(s,b). In contrast, for every fixed ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , the limit s → 0 s\to 0 reveals the Euclidean GD birth barrier. Therefore an Adam-like update may appear SignGD-like at practical mode scales while remaining mathematically GD-like in the infinitesimal limit. For L = 1 L=1 , both iterated limits equal b b .

chunks.section: Depth and the order of limits.
chunks.text: Takeaway. Ideal SignGD makes σ 1 / L \sigma^{1/L} a constant-speed coordinate: positive modes are born, unsupported modes disappear, and nonzero targets are reached in finite time for every depth. The instantaneous Adam approximation inherits this behavior only over the range in which the gradient magnitude dominates ϵ \epsilon . For fixed ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , sufficiently small birth modes recover GD’s finite–logarithmic–polynomial depth transition, unsupported modes develop logarithmic or polynomial decay tails, and final saturation becomes exponential. Thus coordinate normalization controls the phase crossovers.

Muon updates each factor by orthogonalizing matrix updates, that is Z ℓ = U ℓ ​ V ℓ ⊤ Z_{\ell}=U_{\ell}V_{\ell}^{\top} . In the diagonal aligned singular mode model, G = diag ⁡ ( g i ) G=\mathrm{diag}(g_{i}) . Therefore, z i = sign ⁡ ( g i ) z_{i}=\sign(g_{i}) . Thus, for each mode σ ˙ \displaystyle\dot{\sigma} = − L ​ σ q ​ sign ⁡ ( g ) \displaystyle=-L\sigma^{q}\sign(g) = − L ​ σ q ​ sign ⁡ ( ( σ − μ ) ​ σ q ) \displaystyle=-L\sigma^{q}\sign((\sigma-\mu)\sigma^{q}) = − L ​ σ q ​ sign ⁡ ( σ − μ ) \displaystyle=-L\sigma^{q}\sign(\sigma-\mu) reducing it to a scalar sign rule as in SignGD updates. Therefore, Proposition 6 holds for Muon as well. Note that this is a spectral update in matrix space even though the aligned model reduces it to a scalar sign rule as in SignGD updates, and this does not mean Muon has the same global bias as coordinate SignGD. Coordinate SignGD is coordinate-basis dependent. Muon is matrix-basis / spectral-geometry dependent. But in an aligned diagonal model, both reduce to sign dynamics on singular modes. Therefore, Muon weakens low rank bias in the diagonal mode. It controls spectral geometry, not rank directly. A spectral-norm ball constrains the largest singular value, but it does not penalize the number of nonzero singular values. So Muon should not be expected to behave like nuclear-norm minimization.

Thus the rate now decreases with the target singular value μ \mu precisely when 4 ​ L ​ p ​ d 0 < ( μ − s ) ​ ( ( 2 − p ) ​ μ + p ​ s ) 4Lp\,d_{0}<(\mu-s)\bigl((2-p)\mu+ps\bigr) . Thus sufficiently adapted Shampoo can reverse the GD saturation ordering: larger modes, which generated larger cumulative preconditioners, can converge more slowly near their targets. Cumulative Shampoo has no single birth exponent valid throughout training. At fixed positive damping, an infinitesimal mode first follows σ ˙ ∝ μ ​ σ p , \dot{\sigma}\propto\mu\sigma^{p}, with the GD exponent p = 2 − 2 / L . p=2-2/L. After the cumulative state dominates, it follows σ ˙ ∝ σ p − 1 , \dot{\sigma}\propto\sigma^{p-1}, with adapted exponent p − 1 = 1 − 2 / L . p-1=1-2/L. For L = 1 L=1 , the adapted exponent is − 1 -1 . For L = 2 L=2 , it is zero and the adapted singular value grows approximately at constant speed. For L > 2 L>2 , it lies strictly between zero and one, so the adapted phase has a finite hitting time from a vanishing positive mode. Nevertheless, for any fixed d 0 > 0 d_{0}>0 , the complete birth time as s → 0 + s\to 0^{+} remains governed by the preceding GD-like phase. The decay exponent remains p + 1 p+1 in the mode equation and produces a polynomial tolerance time of order δ − p \delta^{-p} for L > 1 L>1 . The saturation rate is β = L ​ μ p d ⋆ \beta=\dfrac{L\mu^{p}}{d_{\star}} , which is approximately 4 L 2 μ − 2 / L 4L^{2}\mu^{-2/L} at saturation. Thus, it can make larger singular modes saturate more slowly, reversing the order during saturation. Saturation depends jointly on depth, target amplitude, damping, and the mode’s accumulated history.

Takeaway. Cumulative Shampoo is a two-stage spectral optimizer rather than a fixed interpolation between GD and Muon. A newly emerging mode first obeys the GD birth law and therefore retains the finite–logarithmic–polynomial depth barrier under fixed damping. After sufficient gradient history has accumulated, the mode enters a target-independent catch-up phase with exponent p − 1 p-1 , weaker singular-magnitude dependence than Muon, and finite adapted-phase hitting time. The same accumulated state acts as inertia during decay: unsupported modes vanish only asymptotically, and previously active modes become harder to remove. Near a nonzero target, Shampoo saturates monotonically and exponentially, but strong accumulation can reverse GD’s mode ordering by making larger target modes converge more slowly.

chunks.section: Relation to exact joint Gauss Newton.
chunks.text: The preceding derivation uses a block diagonal curvature model that inverts each layer block separately. It should be distinguished from exact Gauss Newton over all layers jointly. For one balanced scalar mode, the full product Jacobian with respect to the L L layer amplitudes is J = a L − 1 ​ [ 1 ⋯ 1 ] . J=a^{L-1}\begin{bmatrix}1&\cdots&1\end{bmatrix}. Hence the predictor space curvature is J ​ J ⊤ = L ​ a 2 ​ L − 2 = L ​ σ p . JJ^{\top}=La^{2L-2}=L\sigma^{p}. Exact damped Gauss Newton therefore gives σ ˙ GN = η ​ L ​ σ p L ​ σ p + λ GN ​ ( μ − σ ) . \dot{\sigma}_{\mathrm{GN}}=\eta\frac{L\sigma^{p}}{L\sigma^{p}+\lambda_{\mathrm{GN}}}(\mu-\sigma). Comparing with the K-FAC dynamics derived above, we observe that when damping is zero, both cancel the factorization-induced power σ p \sigma^{p} . They differ only by a common factor L L . With positive damping, the two filters are not identical unless their damping parameters are scaled consistently.

From the dynamics σ ˙ = L ​ σ p ​ ( μ − σ ) σ p + λ KF \dot{\sigma}=\dfrac{L\sigma^{p}(\mu-\sigma)}{\sigma^{p}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}} , the factor σ p σ p + λ KF \dfrac{\sigma^{p}}{\sigma^{p}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}} determines how much of the depth-dependent factorization mobility is cancelled. When λ KF = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}=0 and σ > 0 \sigma>0 , the mobility factor cancels: σ ˙ = L ⁡ ( μ − σ ) . \dot{\sigma}=L(\mu-\sigma). Thus undamped K-FAC behaves like direct gradient flow on the effective singular value, up to the common factor L L . When λ KF > 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}>0 , the cancellation is incomplete for sufficiently small modes.

Let 0 < s < b < μ 0<s<b<\mu . The time required for a positive mode initialized at σ ⁡ ( 0 ) = s \sigma(0)=s to reach b b is T KFAC birth ​ ( s , b ) = 1 L ​ log ⁡ μ − s μ − b + λ KF ​ T GD birth ​ ( s , b ) T_{\mathrm{KFAC}}^{\mathrm{birth}}(s,b)=\frac{1}{L}\log\frac{\mu-s}{\mu-b}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}T_{\mathrm{GD}}^{\mathrm{birth}}(s,b) For an unsupported mode with μ = 0 \mu=0 , the time required to decay from s s to δ ∈ ( 0 , s ) \delta\in(0,s) is T KFAC decay ​ ( s , δ ) = { ( 1 + λ KF ) ​ log ⁡ s δ , L = 1 , 1 L ​ log ⁡ s δ + λ KF L ​ p ​ ( δ − p − s − p ) , L > 1 . T_{\mathrm{KFAC}}^{\mathrm{decay}}(s,\delta)=\begin{cases}(1+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}})\log\dfrac{s}{\delta},&\qquad L=1,\\[8.53581pt] \dfrac{1}{L}\log\dfrac{s}{\delta}+\dfrac{\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}{Lp}\left(\delta^{-p}-s^{-p}\right),&\qquad L>1.\end{cases} For a nonzero target, the time required to reduce the residual from a fixed r 0 r_{0} to δ \delta satisfies from either side satisfies, T KF , ± sat ​ ( r 0 , δ ) = 1 L ​ log ⁡ r 0 δ + λ KF ​ T GD , ± sat ​ ( r 0 , δ ) . T_{\mathrm{KF},\pm}^{\mathrm{sat}}(r_{0},\delta)=\frac{1}{L}\log\frac{r_{0}}{\delta}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}T_{\mathrm{GD},\pm}^{\mathrm{sat}}(r_{0},\delta). Consequently, T KF , ± sat ​ ( r 0 , δ ) = μ p + λ KF L ​ μ p ​ log ⁡ r 0 δ + O ⁡ ( 1 ) . T_{\mathrm{KF},\pm}^{\mathrm{sat}}(r_{0},\delta)=\frac{\mu^{p}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}{L\mu^{p}}\log\frac{r_{0}}{\delta}+O(1).

From the dynamics, we get T KFAC birth ​ ( s , b ) \displaystyle T_{\mathrm{KFAC}}^{\mathrm{birth}}(s,b) = 1 L ​ ∫ s b ( μ − x ) − 1 ​ 𝑑 x + λ KF L ​ ∫ s b σ − p ( μ − x ) ​ 𝑑 x \displaystyle=\frac{1}{L}\int_{s}^{b}(\mu-x)^{-1}\,dx+\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}{L}\int_{s}^{b}\frac{\sigma^{-p}}{(\mu-x)}\,dx = 1 L ​ log ⁡ μ − s μ − b + λ KF ​ T GD birth ​ ( s , b ) . \displaystyle=\frac{1}{L}\log\frac{\mu-s}{\mu-b}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}T_{\mathrm{GD}}^{\mathrm{birth}}(s,b). Thus, the K-FAC birth time decomposes into two terms.

When λ KF = 0 , \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}=0, the mode dynamics reduce to σ ˙ = L ⁡ ( μ − σ ) . \dot{\sigma}=L(\mu-\sigma). The birth time is T KFAC birth ​ ( s , b ) = 1 L ​ log ⁡ μ − s μ − b T_{\mathrm{KFAC}}^{\mathrm{birth}}(s,b)=\dfrac{1}{L}\log\dfrac{\mu-s}{\mu-b} , thus finite time emergence. The exact trajectory is σ ⁡ ( t ) = μ − ( μ − s ) ​ e − L ​ t . \sigma(t)=\mu-(\mu-s)e^{-Lt}. The near-zero birth dynamics are σ ˙ ≈ L ​ μ . \dot{\sigma}\approx L\mu. Hence the undamped K-FAC birth exponent α b \alpha_{\mathrm{b}} is zero. The initial velocity does not vanish with σ \sigma . Undamped K-FAC therefore removes the depth-dependent small-mode barrier. For a common absolute threshold b b and seed s s , ideal Muon has target independent birth time whenever μ > b \mu>b . Undamped curvature flow instead has birth time 1 L ​ log ⁡ μ − s μ − b , \frac{1}{L}\log\frac{\mu-s}{\mu-b}, which decreases with μ \mu . The target amplitude nevertheless remains in the velocity. This distinguishes undamped K-FAC from ideal Muon. Muon removes both the factorization barrier and target-amplitude ordering during aligned birth, whereas undamped K-FAC removes the barrier but preserves target ordering. The cancellation at exactly σ = 0 \sigma=0 requires care. At an exactly zero mode, the undamped Fisher block is singular, so the update depends on the inverse or pseudoinverse convention. The finite birth statement above concerns the limit from a positive seed s → 0 + s\to 0^{+} .

For λ KF > 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}>0 , define the spectral curvature threshold σ KF b = λ KF 1 / p , L > 1 . \sigma_{\mathrm{KF}}^{\mathrm{b}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}^{1/p},\,\,L>1. This is the scale at which σ p ≍ λ KF . \sigma^{p}\asymp\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}. When σ ≪ σ KF b , \sigma\ll\sigma_{\mathrm{KF}}^{\mathrm{b}}, the preconditioning factor is approximately σ p λ KF . \dfrac{\sigma^{p}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}. For a small positive mode with σ ≪ μ \sigma\ll\mu , σ ˙ ≈ L ​ μ λ KF ​ σ p . \dot{\sigma}\approx\dfrac{L\mu}{\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}\sigma^{p}. Thus damped K-FAC recovers the Euclidean GD birth exponent α b = p \alpha_{\mathrm{b}}=p . When σ ≫ σ KF b , \sigma\gg\sigma_{\mathrm{KF}}^{\mathrm{b}}, the preconditioning factor approaches one. The mode then follows σ ˙ ≈ L ⁡ ( μ − σ ) , \dot{\sigma}\approx L(\mu-\sigma), and behaves like direct optimization of the effective matrix. Damped K-FAC therefore has a two-regime birth law: GD-like below σ KF b , \sigma_{\mathrm{KF}}^{\mathrm{b}}, and curvature-corrected above σ KF b \sigma_{\mathrm{KF}}^{\mathrm{b}} . Thus any fixed positive damping restores the Euclidean finite–logarithmic–polynomial birth classification in the infinitesimal limit. For L ≥ 2 L\geq 2 , the limits λ KF → 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}\to 0 and s → 0 s\to 0 do not commute. For every fixed s > 0 s>0 , lim λ KF → 0 T KFAC birth ​ ( s , b ) = 1 L ​ log ⁡ μ − s μ − b . \lim_{\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}\to 0}T_{\mathrm{KFAC}}^{\mathrm{birth}}(s,b)=\frac{1}{L}\log\frac{\mu-s}{\mu-b}.

In contrast, for every fixed λ KF > 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}>0 , the limit s → 0 + s\to 0^{+} is logarithmically divergent at L = 2 L=2 and polynomially divergent for L > 2 L>2 . A numerically small damping can therefore be asymptotically decisive for sufficiently small spectral modes. For L = 1 L=1 , σ ˙ = μ − σ 1 + λ KF , \dot{\sigma}=\dfrac{\mu-\sigma}{1+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}, so damping only changes the speed. For L > 1 L>1 , an exactly zero mode satisfies σ ˙ = 0 \dot{\sigma}=0 under every fixed positive damping because the numerator contains σ p \sigma^{p} . Damped K-FAC therefore also requires a positive seed to initiate growth.

For zero target mode μ = 0 \mu=0 , the K-FAC mode dynamics equation becomes σ ˙ = − L ​ σ p + 1 σ p + λ KF . \dot{\sigma}=-L\dfrac{\sigma^{p+1}}{\sigma^{p}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}. When λ KF = 0 , \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}=0, this reduces to σ ˙ = − L ​ σ . \dot{\sigma}=-L\sigma. Hence T KFAC , 0 decay ​ ( s , δ ) = 1 L ​ log ⁡ s δ , and σ ⁡ ( t ) = s ​ e − L ​ t . T_{\mathrm{KFAC},0}^{\mathrm{decay}}(s,\delta)=\frac{1}{L}\log\frac{s}{\delta},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma(t)=se^{-Lt}. Undamped K-FAC removes an unsupported mode exponentially in time, but the mode reaches zero only asymptotically. Its tolerance time is logarithmic. When λ KF > 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}>0 and σ ≫ σ KF b , \sigma\gg\sigma_{\mathrm{KF}}^{\mathrm{b}}, the decay is still approximately exponential: σ ˙ ≈ − L ​ σ . \dot{\sigma}\approx-L\sigma. Once σ ≪ σ KF b , \sigma\ll\sigma_{\mathrm{KF}}^{\mathrm{b}}, the damping term dominates and σ ˙ ≈ − L λ KF ​ σ p + 1 . \dot{\sigma}\approx-\frac{L}{\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}\sigma^{p+1}. For L = 1 L=1 , p = 0 p=0 and damping only rescales the exponential rate: σ ˙ = − 1 1 + λ KF ​ σ , \dot{\sigma}=-\frac{1}{1+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}\sigma, so T KFAC decay ​ ( s , δ ) = ( 1 + λ KF ) ​ log ⁡ s δ . T_{\mathrm{KFAC}}^{\mathrm{decay}}(s,\delta)=(1+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}})\log\frac{s}{\delta}. For L > 1 L>1 , the final decay is algebraic as shown in Proposition 9 . Equivalently, the singular value evolves as σ ( t ) ∼ ( L ​ p λ KF t ) − 1 / p . \sigma(t)\sim\left(\dfrac{Lp}{\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}t\right)^{-1/p}. Thus positive damping converts the undamped exponential decay into a polynomial tail for every depth L > 1 L>1 .

The curvature threshold governs both birth and decay. Above σ KF b , \sigma_{\mathrm{KF}}^{\mathrm{b}}, K-FAC behaves like direct effective-matrix optimization. Below it, damping restores the same small-mode mobility that appears under Euclidean GD.

The exact saturation times from below and above are, T KF , ± sat ​ ( r 0 , δ ) = 1 L ​ log ⁡ r 0 δ + λ KF ​ T GD , ± sat ​ ( r 0 , δ ) . T_{\mathrm{KF},\pm}^{\mathrm{sat}}(r_{0},\delta)=\frac{1}{L}\log\frac{r_{0}}{\delta}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}T_{\mathrm{GD},\pm}^{\mathrm{sat}}(r_{0},\delta). Consequently, T KF , ± sat ​ ( r 0 , δ ) = μ p + λ KF L ​ μ p ​ log ⁡ r 0 δ + O ⁡ ( 1 ) . T_{\mathrm{KF},\pm}^{\mathrm{sat}}(r_{0},\delta)=\dfrac{\mu^{p}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}{L\mu^{p}}\log\dfrac{r_{0}}{\delta}+O(1). Therefore, the residual dynamics is r ˙ ≈ − L ​ μ p μ p + λ KF ​ r . \dot{r}\approx-L\dfrac{\mu^{p}}{\mu^{p}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}r. This implies K-FAC saturates monotonically and exponentially, with the rate β = L ​ μ p μ p + λ KF . \beta=L\dfrac{\mu^{p}}{\mu^{p}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}. In the undamped case, β = L \beta=L . The rate is independent of the target singular value and of the mobility exponent p p . Under the present time normalization it is proportional to depth; after rescaling time by the common factor L L , every mode has unit saturation rate. With positive damping, the saturation rate has two regimes. If μ p ≫ λ KF , \mu^{p}\gg\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}, then β ≈ L \beta\approx L , so the mode behaves like undamped K-FAC. If μ p ≪ λ KF , \mu^{p}\ll\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}, then β ≈ L λ KF ​ μ p . \beta\approx\dfrac{L}{\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}\mu^{p}. Small target modes therefore recover the GD-like target sensitivity and saturate more slowly. K-FAC always approaches a nonzero target asymptotically in this model. It does not have the finite-time relay behavior of ideal Muon. ∎

Undamped K-FAC removes the depth-dependent factorization exponent from all three phases. Positive modes have finite birth time, unsupported modes decay exponentially, and nonzero targets saturate exponentially. Depth remains only through the common multiplicative rate L L under the present time convention. Positive damping restores depth dependence through p p . For birth, the asymptotic delay changes from finite at L = 1 L=1 to logarithmic at L = 2 L=2 and polynomial for L > 2 L>2 , with exponent p − 1 p-1 . For unsupported modes, damping produces a polynomial tolerance time for L > 1 L>1 . For saturation, small target modes have rate L λ KF ​ μ p , \dfrac{L}{\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}}\mu^{p}, whereas sufficiently large modes approach the undamped rate L L . Thus damping does more than stabilize curvature inversion. It determines which spectral modes experience natural-gradient-like cancellation and which retain the depth-dependent mobility of Euclidean GD. Takeaway. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced small-mode barrier while preserving target-amplitude ordering: positive modes are born in finite time, unsupported modes decay exponentially, and all nonzero targets share the same normalized saturation rate. Additive damping introduces the spectral threshold σ KF b = λ KF 1 / p \sigma_{\mathrm{KF}}^{\mathrm{b}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}^{1/p} . Above this threshold, K-FAC remains curvature corrected; below it, the Euclidean depth laws return. Consequently, any fixed positive damping restores logarithmic or polynomial birth delays, produces a polynomial zero-target tail for L > 1 L>1 , and slows the saturation of small target modes. Damping is therefore an inductive-bias parameter, not merely a numerical regularizer.

We use synthetic deep linear models to isolate the effects of optimizer geometry from nonlinear representation effects. Unless stated otherwise, the effective predictor is W = W L W L − 1 ⋯ W 1 , W=W_{L}W_{L-1}\cdots W_{1}, and all hidden layers have width equal to the input dimension. We use deterministic full batch optimization and do not use weight decay or explicit regularization. All experiments use double precision. We report continuous optimization time as t = k ​ η t=k\eta , where k k is the optimization step and η \eta is the step size or learning rate. For comparisons between optimizers, the learning rate is selected separately for each method because the update magnitudes induced by Euclidean, normalized, spectral, and curvature based methods are not directly comparable. For each optimizer, we sweep the learning rate over a logarithmic grid and select the largest value that gives stable monotone progress without numerical divergence or persistent finite step oscillations away from the target, as well as reaches a similar loss within an admissible range for all optimizers. We then adjust the training horizon so that all optimizers reach approximately the same final training loss. In general, we aim to train for 5000 5000 steps or lower, with each optimizer attaining similar losses. This prevents differences in optimization progress from being interpreted as differences in spectral bias. We plot comparisons of spectra, effective rank, and mode trajectories over time.

Write W = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ W=U\Sigma V^{\top} for a singular value decomposition, with singular values σ 1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ σ r ≥ 0 \sigma_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{r}\geq 0 , where r = min ⁡ ( d 0 , d L ) r=\min(d_{0},d_{L}) . We measure stable rank and effective rank using srank ( W ) = ∑ i σ i 2 σ 1 2 , erank ( W ) = exp ( − ∑ k p k log p k ) , p k = σ k ∑ i σ i . \operatorname{srank}(W)=\frac{\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{2}}{\sigma_{1}^{2}},\qquad\operatorname{erank}(W)=\exp{\left(-\sum_{k}p_{k}\log p_{k}\right)},\,\,p_{k}=\frac{\sigma_{k}}{\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}}. These quantities measure different aspects of spectral concentration and are reported together with the training loss. Thresholds and conventions at W = 0 W=0 are fixed before comparison.

The first setting directly matches the full observation model used in the phase analysis. The input and output dimensions are both 16 16 , and the network has depth L = { 2 , 4 , 8 } L=\{2,4,8\} with hidden width 16 16 . The target matrix is diagonal in the initialization basis, M = diag ⁡ ( 1.00 , 0.80 , 0.60 , 0.45 , 0.32 , 0.24 , 0.18 , 0.12 , 0 , … , 0 ) , M=\operatorname{diag}\left(1.00,0.80,0.60,0.45,0.32,0.24,0.18,0.12,0,\ldots,0\right), and therefore has rank 8 8 . This choice gives several positive target modes with distinct amplitudes together with unsupported modes whose target is zero. We use balanced aligned initialization. For the phase law experiments, positive target modes are initialized at effective amplitude 10 − 3 10^{-3} while zero target modes are initialized at 0.2 0.2 . The corresponding factor amplitudes are initialized as a i ​ ( 0 ) = s i 1 / L , a_{i}(0)=s_{i}^{1/L}, so that σ i ​ ( 0 ) = a i ​ ( 0 ) L = s i \sigma_{i}(0)=a_{i}(0)^{L}=s_{i} for every depth. This initialization preserves the aligned construction used in the theoretical analysis and allows birth and decay to be observed within the same run. The phase statistics are evaluated every optimization step. For birth, we track the local mode dynamics over 10 − 3 ≤ σ ≤ 10 − 1 . 10^{-3}\leq\sigma\leq 10^{-1}. For decay, we follow a zero target mode from its initial active value toward zero. Local exponents are estimated by linear regression over a short sliding window in logarithmic coordinates. The default window contains 21 21 recorded points.

We first evaluate the optimizer dependent spectral dynamics in the full observation matrix factorization setting described in App. F , where the theoretical phase laws apply most directly. (a) Evolution of a weak target mode with μ = 0.18 \mu=0.18 , shown as the learned fraction σ ⁡ ( t ) / μ \sigma(t)/\mu . GD exhibits the factorization induced small mode barrier, whereas normalization and preconditioning substantially accelerate emergence. Fig. 4 provides a broader validation of the theory in addition to the theoretical evaluation done in Sec. 6 . Fig. 5 compares the optimization and rank dynamics. Although the methods eventually reach similar losses and effective ranks, their trajectories differ substantially. GD learns the target modes sequentially and retains a low effective rank for longer, consistent with the small mode mobility factor σ p \sigma^{p} . Adam reduces this separation and activates weaker modes much earlier. Muon produces an even more rapid redistribution of spectral mass, reflecting its normalized spectral update. Cumulative Shampoo initially behaves more like GD but quickly changes regime as its accumulated preconditioner adapts. K-FAC exhibits a smoother evolution in which curvature correction reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales. The stable and effective rank curves therefore mainly differ during the transient phase, while their later agreement reflects the unique full observation target rather than identical optimization dynamics. Figure 5: Optimization and rank dynamics in matrix factorization. All optimizers train the same depth L = 4 L=4 deep linear factorization toward the same rank eight target and reach comparable final training loss. Left: training loss over optimization steps. Middle: stable rank of W W . Right: effective rank of W W . The optimizers exhibit markedly different transient rank dynamics despite converging toward similar final spectra. GD retains a lower rank representation for longer, whereas Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and K-FAC alter the rate at which spectral mass is distributed across modes.

The singular value trajectories in Fig. 6 make these differences more explicit. Under GD, larger target modes emerge first and weaker modes remain close to initialization for substantially longer times. This sequential emergence is the dynamical mechanism underlying its transient low rank bias. Adam substantially compresses these mode dependent delays, while Muon causes the positive modes to follow nearly the same spectral clock until they encounter their different target amplitudes. Cumulative Shampoo exhibits the predicted two stage behavior: early growth remains separated across modes, after which accumulated gradient history accelerates the weaker modes and reduces target amplitude dependence. K-FAC produces the weakest separation between mode trajectories, consistent with curvature correction compensating for the factorization induced mobility barrier. These trajectories illustrate that optimizers reaching similar final solutions can nevertheless pass through very different spectral representations during training. (a) GD (b) Adam (c) Muon (d) Shampoo (e) K-FAC Figure 6: Singular mode trajectories reveal optimizer dependent spectral clocks. GD exhibits strongly sequential learning;Adam reduces these delays, while Muon makes the modes evolve on nearly the same clock until they approach their respective targets. Cumulative Shampoo shows a faster history adapted growth of weaker modes. K-FAC further reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales through curvature correction. The common final amplitudes are determined by the unique full observation target, whereas the transient trajectories expose the distinct inductive biases of the optimizers.

Finally, we vary the factorization depth while keeping the target matrix and effective initialization fixed. Fig. 7 focuses on Adam, cumulative Shampoo, and K-FAC for depths = { 2 , 4 , 8 } =\{2,4,8\} because their state dependent transitions make this interaction particularly explicit. For Adam, increasing depth raises both the GD like and normalized exponents and changes the location of the ϵ \epsilon controlled crossover. For Shampoo, depth changes both the initial exponent p p and the history adapted exponent p − 1 p-1 , while also shifting the point at which accumulated history overtakes the initial damping. For damped K-FAC, increasing depth strengthens the GD like small mode regime through p p , whereas the curvature corrected regime continues to approach exponent zero. The corresponding depth dependence for GD and Muon follows directly from their fixed exponents p p and q q and is consistent with the phase laws reported in the main text. Left: for instantaneous Adam, increasing depth changes both the GD like exponent p = 2 − 2 / L p=2-2/L and the normalized exponent q = 1 − 1 / L q=1-1/L . Middle: for cumulative Shampoo, depth changes the initial GD like exponent p p , the history adapted exponent p − 1 p-1 , and the amplitude at which accumulated history begins to dominate. Right: for damped KFAC, deeper factorizations strengthen the small mode GD like barrier while curvature correction still drives the exponent toward zero above the damping controlled mobility threshold.

Fig. 8 studies the decay exponent of unsupported modes and focuses on Shampoo saturation, where mode order reversal can happen theoretically. For decay, increasing depth changes the small mode geometry through p = 2 − 2 / L p=2-2/L . Empirically, GD, Adam, and cumulative Shampoo follow the predicted increase α d = p + 1 = 3 − 2 L , \alpha_{d}=p+1=3-\frac{2}{L}, so deeper factorizations produce a steeper polynomial tail near zero. In contrast, undamped K-FAC remains close to α d = 1 \alpha_{d}=1 , reflecting its exponential decay law, while Muon exhibits a much weaker depth dependence, consistent with its normalized geometry. Thus depth does not affect all optimizers uniformly: it strengthens the Euclidean style barrier for GD like methods, but has much less impact on normalized or curvature corrected decay. For saturation, we focus on cumulative Shampoo because it is the optimizer for which mode reversal can happen and depth also affects it. Its asymptotic saturation coefficient depends on both target size and accumulated history, β Sh ​ ( μ ) = L ​ μ p D ⋆ ​ ( μ ) . \beta_{\rm Sh}(\mu)=\dfrac{L\mu^{p}}{D_{\star}(\mu)}. As a result, the ordering of saturation rates across target modes need not agree with GD. The right panel shows precisely this effect. For L = 2 L=2 , β \beta decreases with μ \mu , so smaller target modes saturate faster than larger ones. For L = 8 L=8 , the trend reverses and larger target modes saturate faster. The case L = 4 L=4 lies near the transition and becomes weakly nonmonotone. This depth driven change in ordering is the clearest empirical instance of the Shampoo mode reversal predicted by the theory.

All optimizers closely follow the theoretical predictions in general. Right: Shampoo saturation coefficient β \beta as a function of the positive target mode μ \mu for L ∈ { 2 , 4 , 8 } L\in\{2,4,8\} . At L = 8 L=8 , the ordering reverses and larger target modes saturate faster, while L = 4 L=4 lies near the transition. These results show that depth influences not only the size of the phase law exponents, but also the ordering of mode fitting under optimizer state dynamics. In both cases, all optimizers converge to similar rank and loss solutions. But their trajectory shows the difference. For saturation rate, we choose to plot normalized residual x = r ​ μ q ϵ x=\dfrac{r\mu^{q}}{\epsilon} vs normalized saturation rate β L ​ μ p / ϵ \dfrac{\beta}{L\mu^{p}/\epsilon} for ease of representation. Theoretically, near the saturation σ ≈ μ \sigma\approx\mu , so β = L ​ μ p r ​ μ q + ϵ \beta=\dfrac{L\mu^{p}}{r\mu^{q}+\epsilon} . Therefore, the normalized saturation rate reduces to ϵ r ​ μ q + ϵ = 1 1 + x . \frac{\epsilon}{r\mu^{q}+\epsilon}=\frac{1}{1+x}. Fig. 14 examines how the cumulative Shampoo state changes the birth, decay, and saturation dynamics. The birth transition from the initial GD exponent p p toward the history adapted exponent p − 1 p-1 is discussed in the main text. Here we focus on the corresponding decay and saturation behavior. For an unsupported mode with μ = 0 \mu=0 , different values of λ Sh \lambda_{\rm Sh} produce different finite amplitude trajectories, but all curves approach the common asymptotic exponent p + 1 = 2.5 p+1=2.5 for L = 4 L=4 . Even in the case of smaller damping, the deviation from 2.5 2.5 is only in the second decimal place. Thus Shampoo retains a polynomial tail near zero rather than the finite time extinction of ideal Muon. For a positive target mode, the right panel shows each damping level approaches a distinct constant rate, with the empirical curves closely following the finite amplitude prediction. The limiting rate depends on the entire accumulated gradient history and this distinguishes Shampoo from memoryless spectral normalization and explains why modes with similar current residuals can saturate at different rates. Together, the panels show that cumulative Shampoo changes its effective spectral geometry during training while retaining explicit memory of earlier gradient activity.

Fig. 15 illustrates how additive damping in K-FAC controls the spectral dynamics across all three phases. For birth, positive damping restores the small mode barrier. Reducing λ KF \lambda_{\rm KF} shifts this transition toward smaller mode amplitudes, recovering the undamped KFAC regime. For an unsupported mode, the middle panel confirms that stronger damping causes the polynomial regime to appear at larger amplitudes, following the theory. Near a positive target, K-FAC’s saturation rate is nearly constant along the final approach to the target and approaches the undamped value L = 4 L=4 as λ KF → 0 \lambda_{\rm KF}\rightarrow 0 . Thus, K-FAC damping controls not only numerical regularization of the curvature inverse, but also the spectral scale below which GD-like dynamics reappear. Figure 15: Additive K-FAC damping controls the spectral phase transitions. Solid curves show empirical dynamics and dashed curves show the corresponding aligned theory for depth L = 4 L=4 . It shows that λ KF \lambda_{\rm KF} defines a spectral mobility threshold separating curvature corrected dynamics from GD-like behavior.

We next consider a less structured setting in which the effective predictor is trained by underdetermined linear regression as described in App. F . This experiment tests whether the qualitative predictions persist once our simplifying assumptions Assumptions 1 , 2 and 3 are removed. Fig. 16 shows that the optimizers reach comparable training losses and converge to nearly identical final singular spectra. This agreement is important: the pronounced differences observed during training are not simply consequences of one method converging to a substantially different level of fit. Nevertheless, the stable and effective ranks evolve differently. Thus similar terminal predictors need not imply similar spectral learning dynamics. Figure 16: Optimizer dependent dynamics persist in underdetermined linear regression. We train the same deep linear predictor on an underdetermined, nonwhitened regression problem using GD, Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and KFAC. All methods reach comparable final loss and final spectra of W W despite substantially different transient dynamics shown by the stable rank and effective rank throughout training. The optimizer geometry strongly changes how quickly spectral mass concentrates.

The singular value trajectories in Fig. 17 make this distinction particularly clear. GD exhibits pronounced separation between the emergence times of successive singular values, consistent with the factorization induced small mode barrier derived in the aligned setting. Adam substantially compresses these delays. Muon produces a markedly more synchronized growth of the singular spectrum, consistent with normalization reducing mode dependent mobility differences. Cumulative Shampoo also accelerates weaker spectral components after its preconditioner has accumulated sufficient history, while K-FAC produces comparatively smooth growth across the spectrum through curvature correction. These effects remain visible even though the singular vectors are not fixed and the data covariance couples the modes. The experiment therefore supports the interpretation of the theoretical phase laws as mechanisms governing transient spectral learning rather than merely properties of the special aligned model. Exact exponents depend on the aligned reduction, but the resulting qualitative distinctions persist in the more practical underdetermined regression problem. Although all methods approach similar final singular spectra, their transient spectrum differ substantially. The qualitative optimizer dependent dynamics predicted by the aligned phase analysis remain visible even when the empirical data covariance couples singular directions and the exact scalar mode reduction no longer holds.
